div.head: REMOVALS & WAREHOUSING DEPARTMENT

p.hi: A PUBLIC TELEPHONE IS PROVIDED IN THIS DEPARTMENT FOR CUSTOMERS’ USE.

div.p:
HARROD’S HARROD’S DEPOSITORY HARROD’S FURNITURE DEPOSITORY
HARRODS’ DEPOSITORIES AT BARNES.
ONE OF THE SAFEST AND MOST UP-TO-DATE STORAGE PLACES IN THE WORLD.

These spacious Depositories, which are completely isolated, stand in Harrods’ own grounds of 10 acres. They are constructed on fire-resisting principles—are thoroughly dry and well ventilated, thus ensuring the utmost cleanliness and safety for goods in storage. Huge hydraulic lifts take the loaded removal vans direct to the various floors for storage, which saves all straining and risk of damage to goods. Intending depositors are invited to apply for a card to visit this interesting establishment.
REMOVALS BY LAND OR SEA TO AND FROM ALL PARTS OF THE WORLD—ESTIMATES FREE

Inclusive estimates are submitted free of cost at any distance within forty miles. Estimators can be sent to any part of the Country on payment of their third-class return fares, or abroad on payment of reasonable expenses, chargeable only in the event of no business resulting. In cases where it is impracticable or inadvisable to remove furniture abroad in our well-known Railway Vans, estimates will be submitted for the packing and forwarding of it, in cases, to any part of the world.

Our Continental Vans, built especially for this traffic, are constantly in transit and are frequently available on their return journey for our Clients, thus saving the carriage expense on the empty van one way. Favourable quotations can also be had per van load for shipment to any part of America.

The goods are packed at our well-known Barnes Depository, and are shipped direct from Wharf attached, by our own Lighters, which ply between this Wharf and all the London Docks. This is a very great advantage to Clients, as the cases are delivered free on board at a much lower rate than by road, and all the heavy Dock charges attached to the ordinary system are completely avoided.
THIS CONSTITUTES A SAVING OF SEVERAL POUNDS, EVEN ON A SMALL CONSIGNMENT OF FURNITURE
Harrods’ Barges also take delivery from ships on their arrival at London, avoiding all Dock charges here also.

A POWERFUL SPECIALLY-CONSTRUCTED CRANE
has been erected at Barnes for transferring goods from Lighters to our Wharf, and vice versa.
We believe that no other firm in London can offer such advantages to those removing to or from Abroad.

lg.l: A FEW OF THE TESTIMONIALS RECEIVED
DURING THE LAST FEW MONTHS. SELECTED AT RANDOM FROM THOUSANDS WHICH REGULARLY ARRIVE (ENTIRELY UNSOLICITED) FROM SATISFIED CLIENTS.

l.hi: The Originals may always be seen at the Office.

div.p: Removal from Orpington to Kensington, W.

I cannot speak too highly of the very praiseworthy manner in which your men have removed my goods from Orpington to this address. It was a heavy task, and in addition they had bad weather to contend against, but they worked admirably and carefully, and were all most courteous and attentive.
I am pleased to be able to state that the removal was most satisfactory in every way.
Removal from Eaton Place to Depository, thence to Chapel Street, Belgrave Square.
I must say how very well and carefully my things were removed, and shall recommend my friends to employ your firm for removals.
Removal from our Depository to Wrexham.

I should like to write and tell you how pleased I am with the goods that you have stored and packed for me. They arrived here in very good condition indeed, without a scratch. I should also like to mention the services of your foreman you sent down—he was of inestimable value. I can’t speak too highly of your good management throughout.
Removal from Westerham to Depository, thence to Henley House, Upper Warlingham.
Mrs. GIRDLER is much pleased with the condition of the furniture from Messrs. Harrods’ Store and also with the manner in which the removal was carried out.
Removal from Putney to Depository, thence to Bedford Place, Brighton.

I enclose cheque in payment of your account for removal, and beg to say how very satisfactory everything was carried out, and what splendid condition I find everything in. I should also like to say what an exceedingly civil and obliging man the foreman was. I could not have wished any one nicer.
Removal from Upper Brook Street to Nice, France.

I wish to tell you that I am entirely satisfied with the way in which you removed my furniture from London to Nice. Everything arrived in perfect order, and was most carefully packed and unpacked, I was most satisfied with your foreman—he was a very obliging and careful man, and he managed everything beautifully. I had no trouble whatever.
Removal from Hastings to our Depository, thence to Paris.
I am pleased to state that my furniture was delivered in good condition, and to express my entire satisfaction.
Removal from Bury St. Edmunds to Hazelwood, Chandler’s Ford.

I enclose cheque for our furniture removal and have much pleasure in stating that your foreman and his men all worked beautifully and nothing was either broken or damaged, and everything done exactly as I wished. Both Sir Henry Dixon and myself cannot say too much in your foreman’s favour or wish to have a nicer, quieter head man to deal with.
Removal from Foulis Terrace to Haslemere.

Mrs. BARROW is glad to inform Messrs. Harrods that she is very much pleased with the way in which they carried out the removal of her furniture from London to the above address. All the men sent were most careful and obliging, and everything arrived in good condition.
Removal from Cadogan Gardens to Depository, thence to Barham.
The removal of my furniture from your warehouse to Barham has been done to my entire satisfaction, and your foreman showed great attention and civility.
Mrs. CARTER would like to say that the work was very satisfactorily done. Quietly, with despatch and carefully.
Miss BOWYER’S furniture having now been all unpacked, she writes to say how beautifully it has been done, and how well everything has come.
Removal from Harlington to Beaumont Crescent, W.
I have pleasure in enclosing cheque for removal from Harlington, and should like to say we are extremely pleased with the way in which the work has been carried out.
Removal from Eccleston Square to Shopwyke House, Chichester.

Mrs. CLOSE wishes to say that she was extremely pleased with the way her furniture was removed from Eccleston Square. The men sent were most careful in the way they handled and moved the goods, and were particularly civil and obliging.
Removal from Kensington to our Depository, thence to Hastings.
Mrs. BRIDGES writes to say she received her effects, and all was well transacted, and the men most civil and well behaved, and thanks the firm for all they have done.
Removal from Kensington Gardens Square to Leinster Gardens.
I am very pleased with the careful and methodical way in which your men have done the removal, and with their quickness and civility.
I have much pleasure in saying that the removal has been completed satisfactorily.
Removal from Ilfracombe to West Hill, Putney.
Mrs. SEYMOUR is entirely satisfied with the way in which the goods were removed. The men in charge were very civil and obliging, and she has no complaint to make in any way.
Removal from Atherstone Terrace to Homefield Road, Chiswick.

I should like to express to you my appreciation of the manner in which the foreman and men working under him carried out the removal of my furniture and effects from Atherstone Terrace to my new address. They were all most obliging and expert, making everything as easy and comfortable for us as possible.
Removal from Ennismore Gardens and 58 Eaton Square to another house in Eaton Square.

I think it only right to let you know how very pleased Mr. Newman and I are with your Removal Department. The furniture at Ennismore Gardens, which was very heavy and most valuable, and also the furniture of 58 Eaton Square was brought to this house without a scratch, nor are the walls touched. The foreman and men under him worked splendidly and could not have been more obliging.
Removal from Ovington Square to Kidmore End House, near Reading.
We would like to express to you our gratification at the way the removal was effected, and of the courtesy and attention of your foreman and his assistants.
Removal from Cranley Mansions to our Depository, thence to Gloucester Place.

Our furniture has been removed here from Barnes, and I must express to you how highly we appreciate the very excellent way it has been done by your foreman and the men under him. They were most obliging and did everything in their power to make as little noise as possible and were most careful.
Removal from The Cedars, Mitcham, to Catteshall Manor, Godalming.

I should like to express to you my satisfaction at the efficient and expeditious manner in which the work was carried out. Your foreman and the men employed worked with a will, and were one and all most obliging and helpful to us. I should like to say a special word on behalf of the foreman, who took an intelligent interest in everything, and was of great assistance to Mrs. Ritchie and myself.
Removal from Witham to Depository and then to Pett Place, Charing, Kent.

I should like to say how very pleased I am with the careful way in which the removal has been done, and with the excellent way in which all your men have worked. They were most careful, willing and obliging, and worked their hardest to get the house straight as soon as possible. I should like to say how extremely pleased I am with the way my furniture has been stored, and the care that has been taken of it. You have had it stored in your Warehouse for over a year, and it has come out every bit as good as when it went in. There is practically nothing broken and nothing in the least damaged, and what is perhaps more wonderful everything has been kept so beautifully clean. I cannot say enough for your foreman, he worked splendidly, and was most civil and obliging, nothing being too much trouble for him. I don’t think there is a mark on any of the furniture or on the house, which I think is largely due to his excellent supervision and care. With my renewed thanks for the care you have taken of my things.
Believe me, Yours faithfully, (Capt.) F. M. S. PITT.
Removal from Markbeech to Gloucester Terrace, W.
I wish to express my gratitude for the splendid way in which the removal was effected, and for the care, efficiency and civility of the foreman and man under him.
Removal from Charles Street to Lowndes Square.

I am writing to tell you how very satisfied I was with the foreman and the men under his charge who moved us. They were obliging, honest and well conducted in every respect. No china was broken, and nothing is missing.
Removal from Norfolk Mansions to Leith Mansions.
You have always sent me good men for removal, but those sent on the last occasion were the best I ever had. It was a most satisfactory removal.
Removal from Depository to MADRID, SPAIN.

Your foreman completed delivery yesterday of the contents of the vans from your Depository. Everything has been most carefully packed, and I think the condition in which the goods were delivered reflects great credit on your Removal Department. I found your foreman prompt, intelligent, and obliging, and I was thoroughly satisfied with the manner in which he did his work.
Removal from Iver Heath to Depository, thence to Frome.
The work has been carried out to my complete satisfaction. Your men have worked well, and have been most careful and obliging.
I am writing to inform you that the goods which you packed and despatched to Hamilton arrived quite safely. They were exceedingly well packed, and arrived in excellent condition.
Removal from Croydon to Haverhill, Suffolk.

I am pleased to notify you that our removal was effected in an excellent manner—every article arriving in perfect condition, and I should like to strongly commend the foreman for the thorough and assiduous manner in which he carried out the work.
Removal from Albert Hall Mansions to Frensham.

I desire to say how extremely well the business of packing and conveying my things from Albert Hall Mansions to this place was carried out, and how extremely obliging and capable each and all of the men employed about it rendered themselves, for which I thank you.
I should like to say that I consider the move was carried out in a most satisfactory and business-like manner. Nothing could have been better, and I consider the cost very reasonable.
Removal from Ennismore Gardens to Durrington.

I am writing to testify as to the excellence of the work carried out on my behalf by your foreman and his assistant. The furniture removed from Ennismore Gardens to Durrington arrived in perfect order, indeed without blemish. I have nothing to say but praise for the keenness with which they worked in putting the things into the house, and for the civility they showed to everyone here.
Removal from Biggleswade to New Milton, Hants.
The Hon. Mrs. HOLFORD is very much obliged for the way in which the move was done, and the men were most obliging and good.
Removal from Onslow Gardens to Parkstone, Dorset.
I have been very pleased with the way in which the removal of furniture from Onslow Gardens was effected, and with your foreman.
Removal from Kensington Gardens Square to our Depository, stored for three years, and then delivered to Stoke.
I am very pleased with the condition of my furniture, it has come from your Depository in perfect condition.
Removal from Wimbledon to our Depository, thence to Queen’s Gate.

Mrs. KNIGHT wishes to say how satisfactory the foreman and his staff have been over moving her furniture into Queen’s Gate this week after having been warehoused at your Depository since August, 1908.
Removal from Depository to New York, U.S.A.
I beg to say that the van was brought here to-day, and the contents delivered in perfect condition. It was a marvel of good packing, quite worthy of your Removal Department. I thank you.
Removal from Gloucester Street to Fowey.

Mrs. GREENWAY writes to inform Messrs. Harrods that she has duly received the furniture, etc., removed by them from Gloucester Street. Their foreman in charge did the work well, and was very civil and obliging, and Mrs. GREENWAY is glad to say she is quite satisfied.
Removal from Belgrave Road to Depository, thence to Aldershot.
I am very pleased with the way in which you have looked after my furniture, and conveyed it here. Nothing has been broken—which speaks for itself.

The removal has been done very satisfactorily. Not one piece of my very rare and valuable glass and china being broken. This, I think, was due to the excellent management of your foreman and his packer, both of which I should like to commend very highly.
Removal from Maidstone to Thankerton, Lanarkshire.

I take this opportunity of telling you how exceedingly pleased I am with the way your foreman managed the removal of my furniture. Everything was beautifully packed by him, and nothing was either broken or scratched.
Yours truly, A. J. C. FARIE.
Removal from Nevern Mansions to Depository, thence to Patcham, Sussex.

All my furniture and effects were duly delivered at Patcham Place, and I cannot speak too highly of the way everything has been looked after during the two years’ storage. Nothing has been broken, and all the furniture looks clean and nice, and your foreman was most obliging and efficient. He did everything in his power to make things easy for everyone, and I cannot speak too highly of him.
Removal from Eccleston Square to Depository, thence to Chichester.

Mrs. CLOSE has received the goods warehoused, and is very pleased with the way they have been packed and cared for. Mrs. CLOSE wishes to say that the men sent with the goods did their work splendidly.
Removal from Hans Road to our Depository, thence to Abermule, Montgomeryshire.

The furniture has all arrived, and I must say I have never seen things come out of vans in better condition, or better packed than they were. The foreman and his helper were excellent in every way, and most obliging, and if I have to move again I can only hope Messrs. Harrods will undertake to do it.
Removal from Hammerfield, Penshurst, to Lested Lodge, Well Walk, Hampstead.

I beg to express our complete satisfaction with the way in which the furniture was removed from Hammerfield, Penshurst, to Hampstead. There was not a single breakage. The foreman packed the things splendidly and he and all your other men were most civil and obliging.
Removal from Knappe Cross, Exmouth, to Store, thence to 84 Holland Park, W.

This is to certify that your foreman was very careful in handling our furniture recently stored and delivered by your firm. He was most willing and polite in all his work, in fact it is a pleasure to have to deal with such a good foreman.
Removal from 74 Clovelly Mansions, to Castelnau, Barnes.

It gives me satisfaction to inform you that the removal was effected in the best possible way under your foreman, and should any of my friends require moving I shall recommend your firm and also the same staff that you sent for our removal.
Yours truly, CHARLES H. E. RUSH.
Removal from Oakwood Court, Kent, to Leecroft, East Lyss, Hants.

Mrs. and Miss WOOD are very much satisfied with the way in which their furniture has been removed. There are no breakages of any sort, and Miss Wood does not find even any scratches on the furniture. She cannot speak too highly of the foreman, he was most civil and obliging and most careful and clever in managing the difficult pieces of furniture, in short he is a very reliable, trustworthy and efficient man. The packing too of the china, glass and pictures could not possibly have been done better, and both Mrs. and Miss Wood are much obliged to Messrs. Harrods for the excellent manner in which this removal has been carried out.
Removal from St. Thomas’s Hospital to Winchester.
I should like to say that my goods were brought here from St. Thomas’s Hospital in a most satisfactory manner and I found your men, especially the foreman, exceedingly civil, obliging and efficient.
Removal from 34 Hyde Park Gardens, to Clyro Court, Clyro, Hereford.

The removal of my furniture, china, etc., was conducted in a most satisfactory manner. The foreman and men who came here with him were most careful, cheerful and obliging. If I ever have any other removing to do, or if any of my friends want their furniture moved I hope that these men will be available.
Removal from Lexham Harbour to Bexhill.

I would like to add that I am perfectly satisfied with the way the removal was carried out, and I think great credit is due to your foreman from the fact that although the distance was 320 miles there was not a single thing damaged.
Removal from 12 Rutland Court, to 90 Knightsbridge.
I beg to say the goods were most carefully removed, and the men were the best type of workman I have ever had in the house.
Removal from Wimbledon, to Holmhurst, Southboro, Tunbridge Wells.

I am glad to be able to write and tell you how very well your men moved our furniture for us. Not a single piece of china or glass has been broken, and there is scarcely a scratch on any piece of furniture. All the pictures too, have arrived quite safely. The men did their work so quickly and never stopped to talk. I should like specially to mention the foreman, who was most obliging and careful and took the greatest care of the furniture. This is the third time you have moved things for us, and I never wish to have any other firm.
Removal from Machany, Perthshire, to 39 Elm Park Gardens.

I am writing this line to tell you that I am extremely pleased with the manner in which your Removal Dept. have managed my removal. Your men did their utmost to carry out my wishes and were most civil and obliging. The glass and china (of which I have a great deal) were most carefully packed and have arrived in good order.
Removal from 15 Lowndes Square, to Coombe Place, Lewes.
I have to advise you that the removal of my things has been done promptly and nothing has been broken.
Removal from Guildford to The Vicarage, Bembridge, Isle of Wight.

I have great pleasure in saying how efficiently your men carried out their work with practically no damage at all, nothing of the least consequence was broken, and the foreman and his assistants gave every satisfaction.
Removal from 29 Collingham Road to Store, thence to Kilguharity, Dalbeattie, N.B.
Mrs. GLENDINNING wishes to say that your foreman was most careful about the removal of furniture here, and under rather trying circumstances which reflected the greater credit upon him.
Removal from Charterhouse, Godalming, to Deedham, Essex.

I should like to say how thoroughly well satisfied I was with the way in which the work was performed. Among all the glass and china, of which the total amount was large, not a single breakage occurred. The pictures were carefully handled at both ends, and in dealing with the very heavy item of books, the men were patient and thorough from first to last, and they were obliging, civil and careful in all respects.
Removal from Fernbrook, Mann Court Road, Hanwell, to Davenport, Stockport.

I desire to express my appreciation of the excellent and expeditious way in which the removal has been effected. I also wish to give a word of praise to your foreman. He has been most obliging and hard working, and I am sure you could not have sent a better man for the job.
Removal from 2 Cumberland Place, Regents Park, to 88 Lansdowne Road, W.
Mrs. HERTZ wishes to express her satisfaction with the foreman and staff of men sent, their behaviour was very quiet, and they did their best to make the removal as little disagreeable as possible.
Removal from St. Albans to Santa Rosa, Hampstead Green.
I wish to express my great satisfaction with the manner in which your foreman and his assistants performed their work.
Removal from E. Grinstead to Kensington.

Miss COBB wishes to say she is very pleased with the way the moving has been done, and the extreme civility, obligingness and consideration of the foreman, also the quiet behaviour and willingness of the men.
Removal from Kensington to Brookfield, Arundel.
I am glad to avail myself of the opportunity of expressing my satisfaction with the way in which the removal of my furniture was carried out.
Removal from 87 Maida Vale to Store, thence to 20 York Avenue, Hove, Sussex.
I think the goods came out very well indeed after being stored for three years, and please accept my thanks for your attention.
Removal from Fernielaw, Colinton, N.B., to our Depository, thence back to the above address.
We are very pleased indeed with the way you removed the furniture from here to London, and from London back here, and we give all praise for doing it so nicely.
Removal from 12 Roland Gardens, to 8 Kensington Court Gardens, W.

In justice to the men employed by you for our removal to this address, I wish to say that they did their work admirably. They not only did all that was necessary with care and skill, but were most helpful to Mrs. Turner and my servants, and their conduct was all that could have been desired in every way. In the foreman you possess an invaluable servant and no praise would be too great for him.
Removal from Summers Place, Billingshurst, to 193 Queen’s Gate, S.W.

I write a few lines to say how thoroughly pleased I am at the way in which all our furniture, pictures, china, plate, etc., have been moved here from Sussex, and how admirably the work has been done by your foreman and his men at the Sussex end, and by your foreman and his men at this end; nothing could have been better managed and I am glad to be able to write you how well all has been managed.
Wedding Presents packed and dispatched to Bassein, Burma.
I am writing to say that we are extremely satisfied with the way in which our wedding presents were packed by you. We shall highly recommend you for transport packing to all our friends.
Removal from Surbiton to Store, thence to Epsom.

I enclose cheque for removing furniture; everything was nicely done and our furniture none the worse for being stored. I can speak very highly of the men whose business it was to unpack and place the furniture; all were most obliging.
Removal from Upper Chine House, Shanklin, to Montreux, Switzerland.
This is to certify that I am quite satisfied with the men sent by Harrods; everything has arrived in good order and they have been most civil and obliging, and given great satisfaction.

I wish to inform you that your men removed the furniture from my flat in a most workmanlike fashion. The tenants above and below me said they would not have known that moving was being done, had they not seen the cases. The Head Porter told me it was the tidiest and best managed move he had ever seen. A tenant of another flat told me she had been much struck with the excellent neatness re packing cases and general work she saw done from her windows (Flat 2.) I think you may hear from her later on. For myself, I cannot speak too highly of your excellent methods. You moved for us and stored our goods for one year some years ago, and when our furniture came back to us there was absolutely no fault to find, nothing but praise for excellent care shown. Displaying Wedding Presents at the Hans Crescent Hotel.

Removal from Broadstairs, to Upper Norwood, S.E.
May I take this opportunity of saying how exceedingly well and carefully the whole move was carried out. Our thanks are particularly due to your foreman, who was civil and attentive throughout.
Removal from Copenhagen to The Hermitage, Ascot.

I wish to say that I am most satisfied at the way in which the work has been carried out, and at the condition in which everything has arrived. I would particularly commend the foreman, who has shown himself to be a first-rate packer, and I cannot speak too highly of his civility and diligence.

Hints on the Proper Care of a Piano.

In order to assist those who are anxious to preserve the quality, tone, touch, and appearance of their Pianofortes, and obtain the utmost pleasure from them, HARRODS respectfully submit the following suggestions:—

Damp is the greatest enemy of a Piano. The instrument should never be kept in a lower temperature than 60 degrees Fahr. Extreme heat is also injurious. Pianos should not be placed in a direct draught—against the outside wall—adjacent to a window or conservatory, or very near a fire, unless well protected. Should any noise or jarring sound be heard when a Piano is played, it is advisable to ascertain the cause before condemning the instrument. Often it is found to arise from a loose key or candle bracket, or possibly some hard substance dropped inside, or by some adjacent ornaments which sound in sympathy with certain chords and notes. Pianos should be dusted with a soft cloth, and finished with a dry chamois leather to keep the polish bright. Any dulness of polish due to natural oils working through the wood can easily be removed, if attended to at once.
It is important that all Pianos should be regularly tuned and attended to, whether in constant use or not, by competent tuners.

The Tone is produced, exclusively, from full-scale Organ Pipes of the finest quality which are the same as used in the largest Two and Three-Manual Church Organs. The ST. Cecilia Organ is built in several models, but the smallest pattern is far superior to the largest and most costly “American” Reed Organ or Harmonium. It possesses much more variety of tone and also greater carrying power; for blending with and supporting the voice it is unequalled.

The ingenious Pneumatic Action introduced enables the “double bass” stop to give a Pedal Organ effect, actuating from the Manual. On this stop only the lowest note held in a Bass chord is sounded, thus it removes the difficulty of using the Pedals, while preserving the effect, and a perfect 16-feet Pedal Bass is obtained. For those that prefer a Pedal Board, special Models are manufactured.

is a substitute for the most skilled fingers, and will enable anyone old or young to play the Organ with the expression and technique of an accomplished musician, even though never having played an organ before. Extra cost fitted into St. Cecilia Organs £38 10 0

The “Positive” Organ—an entirely British invention and production—was originally designed as a real Organ to replace the Reed Instruments hitherto commonly in use in Village Churches, Mission Rooms, etc. Real Organ Pipes alone are used to produce the tone. A skilled organist is not required, since, from its single keyboard, anyone who can play a Harmonium correctly can obtain perfectly the absolute effect of a Two-Manual and Pedal Organ, and can also transpose.

The precise effect of skilful pedalling is obtained by A Patent Pedal-Bass Stop, which plays in the 16 ft. tone the lowest note only of any chord or succession of chords. The effect of a second manual is obtained by Patent Melodic Solo Stops, whereby the melody of a hymn or voluntary is made to stand out above the accompaniment. To obtain these effects no special skill is necessary. The Transposer enables the pitch of a tune to be changed to bring the music within the reach of the singer or congregation. The “Positive” Organ can easily be blown by the feet or by a hand-blower. The “Positive” Organ occupies no more floor-space than a Harmonium.

div.head: CHINA DEPARTMENT

p.hi: A PUBLIC TELEPHONE IS PROVIDED IN THIS DEPARTMENT FOR CUSTOMERS’ USE.

div.p: This Department is replete with every description of article in CHINA, EARTHENWARE, GLASS and LAMPS. The various sections are tastefully arranged, forming a very brilliant and beautiful array.
by Minton, Copeland, Crown Derby, Cauldon, Doulton, Wedgwood, Worcester, and Limoges in immense variety.
by the same noted Houses, in the newest and best shapes and decorations; unequalled collection.
by the finest Makers; useful and ornamental; worthy of special attention.
from the best English and Continental Houses. Suitable for all parts of the world, special attention having been given for the requirements of India, etc.

Careful attention is given to this important division, and every effort is made to ensure speedy delivery. In case of estimate being given, assistants are instructed to give same in writing, and Customers will oblige by insisting upon this and so avoid any misunderstanding.
These are undertaken and executed in the best and quickest manner by the most experienced workmen.

These are only sent for and returned at Customer’s own risk, although every care and attention will be given to ensure safety. No charge is made for collecting or returning in Districts where our vans call.

Special attention is paid to these orders, and the greatest advantages are given to Customers. An extensive selection of shapes and styles most suitable for Cresting, by all the best makers, on view in Department. Prices can be given personally or by post.

The greatest possible care will be taken in packing goods purchased, but we cannot be liable for breakage after the packages have been despatched or taken from Harrods. Experienced and skilful Packers are employed for Export Orders, and as any breakage that may occur would be due to the usage received during transit, no allowance can be made. Goods purchased for Export in this Department are packed in Casks or Barrels, and only in “Cases” when specially ordered so—as it is found that the risk is reduced to a minimum when packed in the former.
Owing to the unsettled markets, these prices are liable to fluctuation, without notice.
China Dinner Service for Twelve Persons.

p.hi: In the new Arctic Lamps the shade support is stronger, having three arms instead of two; the extinguisher is not so upright and will not fall down if the lamp is moved. The fitting for candlesticks is simpler and obviates any difficulty in removing the plug from the candlestick nozzle.
A tapering adjustable rubber end is now made which will fit in any size nozzle; it does not scratch silver, and is especially suitable for china or glass candelabra.
The Arctic Lamp is constructed on the same principle as a carriage or reading lamp, in which the candle, enclosed in metal tube, is forced up as it burns by means of a spiral spring inside.
It fits in any candlestick, and is made to exactly resemble a wax candle when in use.
For the dinner table decoration it is particularly useful, as the candles remain the same height, yet are burnt to the very end without the slightest waste.
No more guttering candles; no more candle shades taking fire; no smoke or smell when extinguished.

div.p: EXCEPTIONS TO GENERAL RULES OF CARRIAGE

Garden Furniture (Exclusive of Rollers, Mowers, etc.). Delivered free to most stations in England if of the value of 45/0, exclusive of packages. Also to Dublin, Belfast, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Isle of Man, and Channel Islands, if of the value of £5 10s. 0d., exclusive of packages. Goods for Isle of Wight carriage paid to Southampton if of 45/0 value.

Wire Netting delivered free in lots of 70/0 to any station in England and Wales direct from Works. Special prices for Ireland and Scotland. Exact size of mesh cannot be guaranteed, but is the same as accepted by the Trade.
WIRE NETTING IS NOT INCLUDED WITH OTHER GOODS CARRIAGE PAID, UNLESS OF ABOVE VALUE.
Mats are charged cost price, and are not returnable.
Packing for Greenhouses, Summer-houses, Melon Frames, Plant Preservers, Dog and Poultry Appliances, allowed two-thirds if returned carriage paid and in good condition.

Sewing Machines.—Carriage paid on Sewing Machines under the value of £2 to any Railway Station within 100 miles of Harrods. The value of £3 and over to any Railway Station in England and Wales and Channel Islands. Value £4 to any Railway Station in the United Kingdom.
Cases allowed full price if returned carriage paid within one month, with address of sender attached.
Carriage paid to principal stations in England, Scotland and Ireland.
Wringing Machines, Portable Coppers and Washing Machines
Special terms for carriage given on application.

Carrier’s Sheet.—Customers are particularly requested, if unable to examine Contents of Consignments at time of delivery, to sign the Carrier’s Delivery Sheet “Not Examined,” so that claim on the Carrier can be maintained should goods be damaged.
Empty Cases, etc., returned to Harrods should bear the name and address of sender, and should also be advised by post.
For goods to be made to order and all kinds of repairs, etc. Harrods’ printed Estimate form only can be recognised.
A deposit of one quarter the estimated amount is required on any article to be made to a Customer’s order, unless such customer has a deposit account with Harrods.
Carriage paid if within the delivery radius of our own Carts. For the Country, special prices will be quoted according to distance.
Special attention is paid to all kinds of Repairs, goods being called for and returned by our Carts, daily.

Estimates for the repair of Baths, Knife Machines, Mincing Machines, and every kind of Household Machinery. A special feature is made of the re-tinning of all kinds of Copper Goods, which can be returned in many cases the same day.
A COMPETENT MAN WILL BE SENT TO TAKE INSTRUCTIONS FOR REPAIRS.
A charge will be made for collecting and delivering Wringing, Mangling, or Washing Machines, or any other heavy or exceptional article sent for repairs, whether estimate be accepted or not.

p.hi: PUBLIC TELEPHONE IS PROVIDED IN THIS DEPARTMENT FOR CUSTOMERS’ USE.

lg.l: Matchless Flexible Steel Fire Escape Ladder. Price 1/10 per foot.
The ladder is supplied complete ready for attaching to the wall or floor.

div.p:
Thoroughly efficient, strong and light; a child can throw it from a window; no skill required. Perfect safeguard in case of Fire in upper rooms. Carries any weight; occupies very small space. Invaluable for Hotels, Large Business Establishments, or Private Houses.
When ordering please give height from the room floor to the window sill, and the depth from window sill to ground.
The “Accurate” is guaranteed to be the simplest and yet the safest and the most powerful Fire Extinguisher made.
Holds 3 gallons of Liquid, 40 times more effective than water. It will extinguish any kind of Fire instantly.
Throws out a stream 50 ft. long, thereby placing any kind of Fire within easy reach.
Always ready for instant use. Turn upside down, and the action begins at once; reverse and it stops. Perfectly automatic in action. Made of Copper, tested to 350 lb. per square inch.
Also made in 1 and 2 gallons, Price 55/0 and 65/0 respectively.

Harrods’ New No. 1 Pattern Steel Chain Ladder Fire Escape. Made of double Weldless Steel Chain with Iron Steps. Will hold several people at once. Cannot break or burn. Supplied with strong flanges to bolt to floor. A child can throw them out and descend.
No. 2 Pattern, with single side chains, 1/8 per foot run.

The Instantaneous Chute Fire Escape, fitted with Patent Wrought Iron Swinging Frame, can be attached to floor or window and instantaneously swung out ready for use; no lifting required. Takes up very little space and is always ready.
Price for 24 feet, £12/10/0; additional length, 3/6 per foot.

NOTES.—A.—The lean-to houses are made to suit walls with flat, true, or even surfaces to lean against; any provision for projecting piers, window openings, rain-water or drain pipes, &c., entails extra cost. In no case is any lead flashing or fillet provided at back wall; this is at purchaser’s expense.

B.—Every care is taken to prevent breakage of glass in transit, and any glass broken will be replaced free of charge, provided the packages are signed for on arrival as “not examined” or “damaged in transit,” but we cannot hold ourselves responsible beyond the replacement of breakages.
C.—If concrete foundations are preferred in place of creosoted sleepers, they must be provided by purchaser from plans which we would provide.
D.—It is always desirable to paint these houses one extra coat after erection, as the paint is liable to be rubbed or otherwise damaged in transit on rail and in handling when fixing.

These Cabinets are unique in many ways, one distinct advantage being the completely separate chamber for the ice, which is not exposed to the outside or warm air when putting in or taking out edibles; this obviates unnecessary waste, and renders these cabinets both economical and efficient. They further commend themselves to intending purchasers by their convincingly moderate price.

Our new Dry Air Cabinet Refrigerator, constructed especially for us and to our own specification, having great improvements this season to reduce the consumption of ice. The peculiar and scientific construction of this Refrigerator creates a thorough and constant circulation, by which all vapours arising from foods in the provision chamber are condensed in the ice-pan and run off with the melting ice. Supply limited.

THE RATNER PATENT TWELVE-CORNER-BENT SOLID STEEL SAFES. Nos. 2 & 3.

p.hi: Safes are delivered free of charge in London to customer’s house, but should same be required to be hoisted or taken upstairs to flats, &c., an extra charge will be made accordingly.

div.p: These Safes are far superior to the ordinary Four-Corner-Bent Safes.

The body is bent out of one solid steel plate ¼ in. thick; Door ½ in. solid steel plate, strengthened to 1 in., drill-proof over Lock, and secured by a Seven-Lever, Unpickable, Gunpowder and Drill-proof Lock.

The bodies are formed of one plate of steel bent at the twelve corners, thus introducing the important feature of a body which in no way depends upon screws or rivets. This improved construction enables a Safe to withstand a much greater fall than a Safe made in the usual way.
The Fire-Resisting Chambers are 3½ inches thick throughout.
THE RATNER PATENT SOLID STEEL SAFES. LIST 3.
JOINTLESS AT ALL TWELVE CORNERS. Extra Strong.
Body made of tough steel ¼ in. thick, bent at twelve corners, the back being securely riveted on the inner face of the back flange.
Doors ½ in. steel plate, strengthened to 1 in. over Lock and other vital parts.

Lock Case of steel, T section 3 × 2½ × ⅜ in., fitted with numerous steel bolts in front and a continuous fixed bolt at back of door. The door rabbets against a strong bar frame, entirely preventing its being forced open by means of wedges. This frame extends round the whole inside face of the front flange to which it is securely riveted.
Bolt-work secured by Ratner Improved Balance Seven-Lever Unpickable Powder and Violence Proof Locks, protected by a Plate of Ratner Drill-proof Compo. Safe Steel ½ in. thick.

Fire-resisting Chambers.—Lined throughout with wrought steel fire-resisting chambers, 4 in. in thickness, filled with best non-conducting composition, in which is mixed chemical material evolving moisture on the application of heat.
For larger sizes and other pattern safes see Special List, sent on application.

Place the cutting edge of barrel over the centre of the root or weed and with a downward pressure, giving at the same time a turn of the wrist. Upon withdrawing the cutter from the lawn a plug of soil together with the root or weed will be found in the barrel; remove this by means of the plunger, withdraw the weed from the plug of soil, and the plug may then be replaced in the ground, so filling up the hole made by the implement.

This Cabinet is framed in dark American Walnut Wood, with Ash Panels, and has a work bench made of very strong well-seasoned hard wood, which is fitted with a patent Bench-stop, and also with an improved iron Instantaneous Quick Grip Bench Vice. The fittings are made of polished brass, and the Cabinet throughout is of superior strength and workmanship. When closed it makes a handsome and well-finished piece of furniture.

It is 3 ft. 6 ins. long × 2 ft. 6 ins. high; the top forms the Carpenter’s Bench, which is 3 ft. 6 ins. long x 1 ft. 6 ins. wide. An extension piece is sent out with each Cabinet; this can easily be attached and firmly fixed to one end, thus making the Bench 5 ft. long. In this respect it is a great improvement on any combined Cabinet and Work Bench yet placed on the market. It can also be fixed in front of the Bench for Wood Carving or for any other work that requires a strong table.
An improved Combination Tool Cabinet. Joiner’s Bench and Wood-Carver’s Table.

The above engraving shows the Cabinet with the extension attached to it forming a full-size bench 5 ft. long. This engraving also shows the Cabinet open, and it will be seen that the lower part is fitted with racks or clips, in which to place the tools, and that the same use is made of the inside of the two doors. There is also a back to the Cabinet, which can be raised by an ingenious contrivance with the greatest ease, and this is also used as a rack for tools, so that “each tool has its special position.” The value of this arrangement will be at once recognised by all methodical workmen. Every tool will be in its proper place, and can be found when required. On the right side of the Cabinet there is a cupboard to hold the extension piece, and which can also be used to stow away large planes or any other large tools that may be acquired. On the left side are three drawers, as shown in the following engraving, which will be found very useful for any additional tools, or for small work of any description, and in front, under the bench, there is a long shallow drawer, with partitions for nails, screws, brass fittings, etc.
This engraving shows the Cabinet with the back lowered into position, and the doors closed ready for use as a Joiner’s Bench, and fitted with 2 in. Quick Grip Vice.

HATHAWAY’S SHAKESPERIAN END OVER END ECCENTRIC MOTION CHURN

This celebrated Churn is entirely without beaters, the interior of the Barrel being perfectly clean and smooth. The Butter is produced by the sharp and continual concussion caused by the cream falling from end to end, and comes in small granules, the grains of Butter being separated from the milk or cream and kept separate from each other until ready for making up. The whole of the Butter is extracted from the milk or cream and can be churned, washed, salted, and worked in the Churn without the application of the hand. The Butter, as shown in the Granulated form in Churn, is ready to be removed to the Butter Worker for making up.

Nos. 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 specially fitted for Steam, Electricity, Horse, or Water Power if required. Prices on application. It is recommended that Churns be ordered of good size to admit of the expansion of the cream in churning.
N.B.—In ordering Churns customers should be careful to select the right size they require, as when a Churn is once ordered and has left our Works we do not under any circumstances exchange it for any other size.

BRADFORD’S NEW PATENT SINGLE-HANDLE FASTENER, For “Diaphragm” and “Endundend” Churns.
Awarded Silver Medal, Royal Agricultural Society of England, 1910.

This New Patent Lid Fastener marks a further step towards simplification and speed in fittings connected with barrel Churns, one end of the barrel of which is formed by the lid of the Churn. A rod, with a cam at either end, is attached to the lid, and when the two swivel links which are attached to the Churn are placed over the cam a single movement of the handle completes the fastening of the lid and ensures a perfect and reliable joint. The lid is unfastened and removed with equal facility. Our “Diaphragm” Churn is the original Two-Fastener Churn. This fastener is a further improvement, and is rightly called a Single-Handle Fastener.
The Churn here illustrated is fitted with the ‘Diaphragm’ Dash. The most Simple and Latest in Churn Fasteners.

The “Simplex” is so constructed that the Benzoline which is required to keep the Platinum Point red-hot is utilized also for heating the Point at first, thereby dispensing with the Spirit Lamp used with the “Original.” The flame is blue and perfectly smokeless. By turning the round Vulcanite Disc to certain marks, the Benzoline Gas supplies the Lamp, or it may be directed, by a turn, into the heated Point, and keeps this red-hot. By another turn, all escape from the bottle is shut off, and this can now be safely packed away and carried in any position.
The “Simplex” has a well-finished Nickeled Bottle.
The “Simplex,” with Standard “A” Point (No. 276) complete, 22/6 each. Extra Points for the “Simplex,” 8/4 each.

div.head: ELECTRICAL ENGINEERING DEPARTMENT.
div.p:
An excellent method of lighting Country Houses is by Air Gas, which is becoming very popular on account of low first cost, small upkeep, and the general satisfaction obtained from its use. Air Gas can be made available for illuminating establishments of all sizes, and especially those of moderate dimensions, being quite simple in manufacture and free from risk of explosion. Harrods have tested every make of machine in the market, and can strongly recommend Cox’s system. These machines are low in price but excellently made.
A 30-light machine can be run at its full capacity upon one gallon of petrol for 4½ hours, each light giving about 100 c.p. It should be understood that each light can, on all plants, be subdivided into lights of less candle-power.
Size 0—Complete Producer Plant, to supply up to 15 lights of 100 c.p.

We undertake the installation of complete ACETYLENE plants, and send an expert to advise Clients or give an estimate for work required to be done.

The ACETYLENE FLAME is peculiar and good in its affording a light more like that given by the sun (daylight) than any other artificial light; both colours and tints can be readily matched, and pictures can be appreciated by it. No other artificial light has this quality.
The products of combustion are the same as from coal gas, but only about one-twelfth the volume for a given light. The Acetylene flame is quite smokeless.

It is a safe light, Acetylene being less poisonous than coal gas. As the issue from an open burner is so small, it would have to be left open for a very long period in a closed room to render the air dangerous to breathe. The slow issue of gas is also an element of safety against explosion, for a burner would require to be left open several days to make an explosive mixture in a room.
A good and reliable Generator is of course necessary to ensure the foregoing.
New piping, if required, is inexpensive, as it only needs to be one-third the size of piping for coal gas. Small pipes are inconspicuous when run in finished rooms.

The Generator here illustrated is the Cavendish “A.B.C.” (automatic), and is considered the most simple and economical now before the public. The attention needed that of a lad or odd man, is not more than ten minutes daily, and much less than the time required by lamps. There are no mechanical parts except two water taps, and nothing to get out of order or readily wear out. The generating apparatus consists of the central gas holder, on each side of which is a generating chamber and a condenser. The generating chambers are in duplicate and work independently, which is a great advantage in admitting of re-charging always being done in daylight without wasting unspent material. The gas given is cool and clean. There is no compression of gas or variable pressure from the holder. There is a positive working escape pipe if the holders should be carelessly over-charged. The Insurance Companies charge no extra premiums where this Generator is used.

div.p: Ferranti Electric Disc Stove for boiling, grilling, and toasting.

Very popular because of its general usefulness and portability. It will accomplish all the work usually done on a gas ring, with greater cleanliness and economy. Scientifically designed so that no heat is wasted. The best results are obtained with clean flat-bottomed utensils. An extension plate to allow two or three utensils to be used at one time, together with silver grill and toaster, may be obtained in Harrods’ Electrical Showrooms.

Single Heat Disc Stoves (for voltages up to 250 volts): Diameter of top plate, 7 in.; weight of complete stove, 6½ lbs.; current consumption, 700-800 volts; cost per hour (electricity at 1d. per unit), ¾d.; time required (stove hot) to boil 1½ pints of water, 7 minutes.
Price (including connector and 9 feet of flexible cord), 32/0
Ferranti Electric Duplex Disc Stove for boiling, simmering, toasting, and baking.
This apparatus forms the basis of a complete kitchen equipment.

The Heating Discs are extremely useful for many culinary operations, and are made flush with the main plate so that several utensils can be placed half on for simmering on the low heat. Each disc can be switched on separately and regulated high or low, thus providing five ranges of heat in the oven, viz.:—1 disc low, 200 watts; 2 discs low, 400 watts; 1 disc high, 800 watts; 1 disc high and 1 disc low, 1000 watts; 2 discs high, 1600 watts. The frame is of cast iron, well enamelled, with nickelled edges. The whole apparatus is strong enough for rough kitchen use and yet well finished to encourage cleanliness and care. The electrical gear is extremely simple and reliable, and well protected in every way. Length, 25 in.; breadth 18 in.; weight approximately, 100 lbs. Each disc has a maximum capacity of 800 watts on the high heat and 200 watts on the low heat.
Price (including 3 yards of strong flexible cable), 6 Guineas

Ferranti Electric Fire gives a clean bright heat in five minutes, and is the most convenient form of Heater obtainable. The bright glowing heat of the centre Disc is concentrated and reflected, making possible a comforting comparison with a cheerful coal fire. The Electric Fire can be used for making toast in the old fashioned way, and grilling can be accomplished with a Dutch oven as before an open fire. The Concave Reflector is pivotted so that it can be tilted horizontally, in which position a small kettle of water can be placed on the Quartz Disc and boiled in six minutes.
Reflector: Polished Copper. Frame and Ornaments: Bronzed.
Wire guard, 10/6 extra; current consumption 900/1000 watts; height, 28 in.; weight, 28½ lb.; diameter of reflector, 18 in. Consumes less than one unit per hour.

Ferranti Electric Breakfast Cooker, consists of 1 Disc Stove 7 in. diameter, 32/0; extension plate (silver plated), 10/6; 1½ pint aluminium kettle, 8/6; 1½ pint aluminium saucepan, 8/6; griller, 10/6; toaster, 2/6; price, complete, £3 12 6 The illustration also shows a large aluminium and asbestos tray (dull finish with bright beading), 24 in. x 18 in., price 21/0 extra. The disc stove uses 800 watts or 8/10ths of a unit of electricity per hour. Time required to boil 1½ pints of water is less than 15 minutes, even if the stove is quite cold to begin with. The Griller is ready for cooking bacon, steaks, chops, etc., in a few minutes after being placed on the hot disc. The Griller can be set upon a dish on the table and food served “direct from the grill.”

div.p: Harrods are famed for the quality of their Groceries and Provisions, and regularly execute orders for customers in all parts of the Kingdom. They also purvey for Clubs, Hotels, and similar institutions, as well as for Yachts, House Boats, Camps, &c.
Weekly Price Lists giving the latest prices of comestibles are issued each week, and afford practical assistance in the selection of requirements.
An inspection of the Food-Stuff Departments cannot fail to impress the visitor with the absolute cleanliness and the strict adherence to hygienic principles which prevails everywhere.

Any that are delivered will be at Consignee’s own risk.

Complaints are frequently received of the quality of the oil supplied, but, upon investigation, it is found in nearly every case that the lamp is in fault. Customers making use of Kerosene or Crystal Oil for lamps are recommended to observe the following precautions. By so doing the liability to explosion will be avoided, and the best light obtained.
No lamp should be used in which there is a possibility of the oil coming into contact with the flame. The well should not be filled too full.
When a lamp has been unused for a considerable time, the well should be drained and the whole thoroughly cleaned, filled with fresh oil, and fitted with a fresh dry wick.

Special attention should be paid to the size and quality of the wick, which should exactly fit the burner (so as to move up and down easily, but not loosely), and should be of soft texture, and not too highly plaited.
When putting out a lamp, care should be taken not to screw down the wick low enough to allow any of the charred portion to fall into the well.
The lamp should not be blown out, but the wick should be turned down very low and left to go out.
Mineral Oils are accepted by Railway Companies on the days specified below, and all orders should reach the Stores on the day previous to ensure dispatch.

Directions for Turtle Soup.—The preparation requires to be soaked in cold water for three days (changing the water daily), when it extends to three or four times its present bulk or weight—becoming exactly similar to the Calipash and Calipee obtained from the fish after being killed. It is then to be cut into pieces of about an inch square, added to a suitable stock, and cooked until quite tender. One pound weight of Dried Turtle is sufficient for three quarts of soup. A glass of dry sherry added to each quart of soup will be found an improvement. Lemon juice and cayenne to taste.

div.head: BAKERY DEPARTMENT
div.p: Harrods have gained special distinction in this Branch, and supply exclusive and artistic Cakes from 10/6 to 50 guineas each at the uniform price of 1/6 per pound. Harrods make all their Cakes on the premises in their own bakery, and employ for this work only the most skilful and successful English and Continental Specialists. They supply one standard quality of cake only, the choicest that can be made, and of delicious quality and all-round excellence. The Cakes are encrusted with a thick layer of pure Almond Paste, artistically iced and piped with white sugar, which is made by a new process rendering it EASILY cut (not the usual hard icing), handsomely ornamented with silver decorations, etc. They are sold by weight at 1/6 per pound, unless otherwise arranged, and this price includes a finished Cake with simple decorations. Top centre ornaments and fuller decorations extra. Cakes intended to be decorated with natural flowers, and on request, are suitably piped to admit of this. To enhance the appearance of Cakes, a silver stand and saw can be hired at a nominal price, according to size; and, unless specially instructed to cut in wedges, all Cakes are sent out intact.

As direct dealers with prominent Wine Shippers and Distillers, Harrods hold the reputation of always having a good Stock of Wines of the most favourable vintages. The prices quoted will be found, to compare favourably with other Wine Merchants.
Practical men sent to bin away and arrange cellars for Town and Country at a moderate charge. Railway expenses will be charged extra for the latter.

Cellar Temperature. It should be dry and well-ventilated, not draughty; temperature not to be below 50° Fahr. nor exceed 60° Fahr. All Wines binned away on their side (Port with chalk mark uppermost). Crusted Wines should be decanted before using. When bottles are uncorked it is essential to wipe neck of bottle.

RECIPES FOR WINE CUP, CYDER CUP AND COCKTAILS.

div.p: CLARET.—To 2 bottles Claret add 3 bottles Soda Water, a liqueur glass of Sherry or Orange Curaçao, the peel of a Lemon, powdered Sugar to taste, a few slices Cucumber Peel, or, instead, some sprigs of Borage.
CHAMPAGNE.—To each bottle Champagne add 2 bottles Soda Water, a liqueur glass Orange Curaçao, a few slices Cucumber Peel (Maraschino may be substituted for Curaçao).

CYDER CUP.—To each bottle Cyder add 2 bottles Soda Water, a wine glass Brandy, and the peel of a Lemon with a sprig of Borage. A small amount of Sugar to be added to taste, if a dry Cyder.
When the above Cups are completed, they should be put on the ice, but on no account should ice be put into the cup.

MANHATTAN COCKTAIL.—Half fill a tumbler with chipped ice, add 4 drops Angostura Bitters, half a wine glass Scotch Whisky, half a wine glass of Italian Vermouth, half a glass Curaçao, half a liqueur glass plain Syrup, well shake, put in a piece of Lemon, and serve.

BRANDY COCKTAIL.—Half fill a tumbler with chipped ice, add 4 drops Angostura Bitters, 1 wine glass Brandy, half a wine glass Curaçao, half of Syrup, well shake, put in a small piece of Lemon, and serve.

The Renowned Scotch Whisky of Great Age.

p.hi: V.O.H. Special Reserve, of Great AGE.

Has the peculiar but most pleasing palatable flavour which is a result of being matured in wood for a considerable number of years. It is imbued with those exhilarating properties which stimulate the brain to healthy activity, and it will appeal to connoisseurs as being a Scotch Whisky in its truest Essence and Spirit.

div.p: These Whiskies, which are the property of Messrs. Harrods, will at once appeal to connoisseurs as rich and mellow blends of exceptional purity. They are supplied to a large clientele, who prefer them to Whiskies quoted at much higher figures because of their absolute uniformity in quality, a feature so often lacking with many at the same price. Harrods have never less than 3,000 gallons in stock maturing in the wood, and they guarantee every bottle of their V.O.H. Special Blend 8 years old, and their V.O.H. Reserve a Whisky of much greater age.

Harrods highly recommend these two Blends to discriminating critics who desire a genuine Old Highland Whisky, possessed of exhilarating qualities without the detrimental after-effects associated with the ordinary run of spirits.

div.head: GENERAL HIRE DEPARTMENT.
div.p: SUPPLY CUTLERY, PLATE, CHINA, GLASS, TABLING, etc., etc., ON HIRE, SUBJECT TO THE FOLLOWING CONDITIONS:—
No. 1.—Immediately upon delivery of goods the Customer becomes responsible for any loss or damage until they are again taken charge of by one of Harrods’ assistants.

No. 2.—That the accompanying Lists of Prices are fixed for one day’s Hire, the Goods being delivered on the day required for use and re-collected the day following. If the articles are to be re-collected the same day after use (necessitating special collection), an extra charge will be made. Should the Articles not be given up on application, additional Hiring will be charged.

lg.l: No. 3.—That the goods may be Hired for any specified period, the charges being estimated, when the price is not specially given, in the following manner, viz.:—
One day, as indicated in List.
Two days, as one and a half days.
One week, as twice one day.
Two weeks, as three times one day.
Three weeks, as three and a half times one day.
One month, as four times one day.

div.p: No. 4.—That when Goods are conveyed by other than Harrods’ vans the Customer is responsible for any loss or damage during transit.

No. 5.—That when Goods are Hired for a term exceeding one week, Notice must be given to the Hire Department at least two days before the Goods are to be removed, otherwise Customers are responsible for such goods, and also for Hire for such time as they may be detained.
No. 6.—All Men servants engaged from Harrods are considered as servants of the Hirer, and the firm do not hold themselves responsible for any breakage or loss while these are in the Hirer’s employ.

No. 7.—Goods on Hire are not delivered free beyond our Town delivery, excepting small parcels, which will be sent free within our Suburban delivery, but an extra charge will be made for the delivery of bulky Goods. Carriage on Hired Goods sent to the Country will be extra.

div.head:
Section IV.
FASHION DEPARTMENTS
div.p: The Departments devoted to Fashion have a particular fascination, the name Harrods being a cachet with well-dressed people for correct and distinctive attire.

Their fashion experts regularly visit the Continental markets. They have established agencies in the leading centres which keep them informed of the trend of fashion, and constantly feed them with novelties.

Harrods have developed the manufacturing side of their fashion business to such an extent that they now produce in their own workrooms a great number of fashionable garments, including gowns, coats, blouses, millinery, and underwear, many of original design as well as replicas of selected Paris models.

This development of manufacture not only tends to improve quality by giving Harrods the entire supervision of the materials and workmanship, but also lessens the cost to customers, all middle profit being obviated by this method of supplying direct.

div.head: SILK DEPARTMENT.

p.hi: Fashion demands a lavish use of these exquisite materials in every lady’s toilette. Many and varied are the weaves stocked at Harrods. The range of beautiful and artistic colours—many exclusively dyed—surpasses any collection previously offered. Every shade and tone that has a place in the present modes is stocked in many qualities.

Not only in exclusiveness of material does Harrods’ supremacy lie; their value also is never found lacking. The enormous output they enjoy opens every market to them, so all French, Swiss and Japanese silks are imported direct. The British silks also reach Harrods’ counters without the aid of the middleman, thus ensuring lowest prices to Customers.

div.p: The largest and best selected variety of high-class Artificial Flowers and Feathers in London to select from. div.head: DYEING & CLEANING DEPARTMENT

p.hi: A PUBLIC TELEPHONE IS PROVIDED IN THIS DEPARTMENT FOR CUSTOMERS’ USE.

div.p: HOW TO SEND GOODS.—Customers sending Goods for Cleaning or Dyeing are particularly requested to enclose in the parcels their Name and Address, with full particulars and instructions.
Parcels sent from the Country should always be advised per post, as by so doing delay and miscarriage are prevented.

DELIVERY AND COLLECTION.—Goods are collected and delivered free in London and Suburbs, but the articles must be in readiness, securely tied up, to go by the carts when they call, as the large delivery and collection of Goods will not permit of any delay. Name and address should be enclosed in each parcel, also instructions.

NON-LIABILITY.—Harrods give notice that Goods are received only on condition that they be not held responsible for loss arising from any fault there may be in the material, and which is developed in the process of dyeing or cleaning, or for shrinkage; every possible care is exercised with goods which are faded and tender, but all work undertaken at OWNER’s RISK.
CANNOT GUARANTEE.—Goods ordered to be dyed to match pattern the exact shade cannot be guaranteed, but Harrods always dye as nearly as possible to the shade selected.

The following prices have been carefully prepared, and may be taken as a safe guide, although Harrods do not hold themselves bound to them in all cases, owing to the immense variety in style and quality of articles sent. A definite estimate can always be given before putting work in hand, and quotations for quantities supplied on application.
Chemical and Wet Cleaning Charged Same Prices.
Tussore, China, and other Soft Silks
Old Tapestries Cleaned, 2/0 to 4/0 per square yard.
Lace and Muslin, goffered or pleated one side

p.hi: All the above Finished by Special Machinery.

div.p: Harrods have fitted up in this Department the most approved machines for Polishing Dance Cloths, Carpet Covers, and Stair Damask.
They have also a special method for drying, which ensures perfect freedom from Creases and an even surface.
Chintz Glazing is also a special study; and those requiring good work at moderate charges would do well to give Harrods a trial.
Cretonnes, Chintzes, and Cotton Goods seldom clean successfully by the Chemical process. Harrods therefore claim to use their discretion as to the methods most suitable.
The White ground of Cretonnes and Chintzes can be tinted with a very pretty effect, and without changing the colour in the design. This is an advantage where the colours are washed out or faded.

Ordinary (or Wet) Cleaning is specially studied, as many articles when stained or discoloured by wear can only be restored to anything like their original condition by this method. A number of new appliances enable Harrods to Clean and Finish the work in a superior manner.

After many experiments a process has been discovered whereby we are able to dye Silk goods without unpicking or removing trimmings, and by the adoption of this method the original lustre of the fabric is maintained.
The result is an “Equal to New” appearance of such things as Brocades, Satins, and Silks.

This method of treatment is particularly recommended for valuable Ball and Evening Dresses, Silk Tea Gowns, Mantles and Costumes, as it involves no risk of deterioration of material. Prices upon application.

div.p: As this Department is in charge of experienced lace cleaners and finishers, all laces are carefully cleaned and got up in the best style.
Antique and Modern Lace of every description in Handkerchiefs, Collars, Cuffs, etc., beautifully cleaned or tinted and finished as when new.
Maltese, Mechlin, Limerick, and Valenciennes Laces have the edges carefully wrought out and the patterns raised as in the manufacture.
Lace Shawls, Jackets, Veils, etc., dyed and finished.
Lace Dyed all colours. Black Lace re-dyed. All laces are done at owner’s risk, and the value of expensive lots should be notified, to ensure special attention.

It cannot be too widely known that, after much patient experiment, Harrods have designed and perfected a machine for softening and imparting a clear surface and the original lustre and brilliance to silks after dyeing.

Everyone knows the complaints so general about Dyed Silks—viz., that they are hard and papery, and have lost their former suppleness. This can no longer be said about Silks, either for Dresses or for Upholstery, dyed by Harrods.

N.B.—Owing to the use of chemicals in the production of many Glacé and other makes of bright finished silks, the traces of which cannot be detected before immersion, Harrods do not undertake any risk in cleaning or dyeing; in all cases these goods are treated with the greatest care to ensure a satisfactory result, but only at owner’s risk.

div.head:
Section V.
SERVICE DEPARTMENTS
SERVICE DEPARTMENTS
div.p: BANKING INSURANCE SAFE DEPOSIT RESTAURANT ESTATE AGENTS VALUATIONS AUCTIONEERS MOTOR HIRE THEATRE TICKET AGENCY LIBRARY EXPORT and SHIPPING PASSENGER TICKET BUREAU

At Harrods there is a wonderful series of separate Service Departments run for the convenience of clients. These undertake the insurance of life, property and servants, buy, sell or let houses and estates, buy or sell stocks and shares, let safes in which to keep valuables, let out on hire such useful things as pianos, cutlery, plate, linen, &c. Harrods will at the shortest notice supply everything for social functions and carry same through without trouble to the hostess. One can book seats at the Theatres, secure tickets for railway journeys, book sea passages, despatch household and other property to any part of the world. You can get your hair dressed, hire a carriage or motor car, lunch or dine on the premises, enjoy the club and reading room, join an up-to-date library, advertise in any paper, warehouse your furniture and effects, store furs, tapestries, etc., in a specially constructed cold-air chamber, and open a banking account.

div.head: BANKING DEPARTMENT
div.p: CURRENT ACCOUNTS—Current Accounts are opened for Shareholders and Customers or friends introduced by them.

Interest at the rate of 2½ per cent. per annum free of Income Tax is allowed upon the minimum monthly balance, provided it is not under £20, and such interest is credited annually in the first week in January.
No Commission charged for keeping Accounts, but the opening lodgment must not be under £20, nor the minimum balance less than £10.
Cheques are made up in books of 30, 60, 100, and 120, and will be charged to clients at the actual cost of stamps—viz.:— 2/6, 5/0, 8/4, and 10/- respectively.
Pass Books will be made up weekly or otherwise to suit clients, but in all cases should be returned every quarter-day for comparison with the Ledgers.
DEPOSIT ACCOUNTS.—Money is received on deposit in sums of not less than £5, nor more than £300, subject to seven days’ notice of withdrawal.
Interest free of Income Tax is allowed from date of deposit to date upon which withdrawal notice expires, and is paid half-yearly—viz., 30th June and 31st December.
The Directors reserve to themselves the power to return deposits or change the rate of interest upon giving one month’s notice.
Any change of address should be notified to the Manager of the Banking Department to ensure the interest being remitted direct.

Deposit Accounts may not be drawn upon by Cheque; but at any time a sum may be transferred to Current Account upon receipt of Deposit Note with the necessary instructions written thereon, duly signed by the Depositor.
Country or other drafts will be received and placed to credit of account when realised, without charge for clearing.
Dividends, Annuities, Pensions, etc., received and placed to credit of account or remitted as may be arranged.
Circular Notes and Letters of Credit obtained.
BILLS FOR COLLECTION.—The collection of Bills on London and Provinces, either Clean or Documentary, is undertaken on the following terms:—
A Commission of 1¼ per centum, which covers all ordinary expenses of collection and remission, but a Minimum of Two Shillings and Sixpence is charged on small Bills of £10 and under.
Bill Stamps, Notarial Expenses, &c., extra if incurred.
Instructions should accompany Drafts as to procedure in case of non-payment.

STOCKS AND SHARES.—For the convenience of Shareholders and Customers the Directors have arranged for the Manager of this Department to afford all necessary information as to prices of Shares to intending Buyers or Sellers, and to transact business on their behalf with the Company’s Brokers, the terms for which will be forwarded on application to the Manager of the Department.

p.hi: Remittances may be made by Cheque, Bank Notes, Postal Orders, or Coin, but should in all cases be registered.

div.p: A personal interview is desirable in the opening of an account, but this formula may be dispensed with by filling up the form provided for the convenience of Customers residing at a distance from the Stores, which will be forwarded on application.

p.hi: Banking Hours: Nine to Six. Saturdays: Nine to One.

div.head: Posts & Telegraph office
div.p: Situated near the Banking Department and Chief Cashier’s Office in HARRODS’ ROYAL EXCHANGE.
Customers may send Telegrams from and have their Letters addressed to the Royal Exchange.

NOTICE.—An Appointment Board is hung in the Royal Exchange to enable Customers to leave Notes for their Friends. The Royal Exchange is such a recognised rendezvous that this proves a very convenient and much-appreciated innovation.

div.head: INSURANCE DEPARTMENT
div.p: Harrods’ Insurance Department occupies a unique position in the Insurance world, acting as Agents for all the principal Insurance Companies, and being represented at Lloyd’s by an expert Manager. Every class of Insurance is undertaken, and information, expert advice, and quotations freely tendered to Clients. Harrods have no preferential arrangement with any Insurance Companies or Underwriters, but advise their Clients purely on the merits of the various offices, thus obtaining always the best possible terms consistent with perfect security. (Situated on Second Floor, take Lift in Carpet Dept.)

div.head: HARRODS SAFE DEPOSIT
div.p: AS SAFE AS THE BANK OF ENGLAND
Harrods’ Safe Deposit—isolated from the outside world—is absolutely secure against Burglary, Fire, Explosives, or Damp.
Never a day passes but some daring burglary is committed—someone’s much valued treasures or heirlooms are stolen; insurance cannot replace these nor cover their loss when sentimental reasons prevail.

Harrods are continually receiving letters from Renters in their Safe Deposit, whose houses have been broken into. Yet they are happily congratulating themselves because their valuables are in safe keeping at Harrods’.

THE most up-to-date Safety Vault in the World. It contains every appliance of mechanical ingenuity known to science, invented to outwit the most accomplished safe breaker, in addition to its absolute security from Fire, Explosives and Damp. Over 30,000 boxes, plate chests, etc., have been collected and delivered to customers during the last 12 years. The list of Renters includes, among other notabilities, an Egyptian Princess, whose deposit in Jewellery was valued at over £600,000.

p.hi: Ratner’s Patent Compo Steel, which is used throughout, has resisted the most perfect drill manufactured. Even if the Stores were consumed by flames the Safe Deposit Vaults and contents would be uninjured.

The main doors guarding the Safes and Strong Rooms have upon them, in addition to three unpickable and gunpowder-proof locks, Time or Clock Locks, so that when the Deposit is closed at night, under no circumstances can the doors be opened again until business hours next morning (not even by those in possession of the keys), or such other time as the clocks may be set for by the order of the Managing Director to cover Sundays and Holidays.

The sure and safe method of preventing loss either from Burglary or Fire is to deposit your valuables in Harrods’ Safe Deposit—it is impregnable to the most skilful or daring thief, and is constructed to withstand the fiercest fire.
Not only is absolute safety assured, but the mind is set at rest, knowing that one’s valuables are in safe custody.
What The Standard says about HARRODS’ SAFE DEPOSIT

“It is satisfactory to note that the steps taken by the well-known West End establishment, Harrods, to meet this requirement in their section of the metropolis has met with well-merited success. ‘It is difficult to estimate the amount of wealth in our keeping,’ said the manager of their Safe Deposit Department. ‘The depositors do not always take us into their confidence, but we learn something occasionally through the inquiries of the insurance companies. During the trouble in Portugal we had a dress-box brought here which was filled with gold plate. Now and again a depositor will display the contents of a chest. During the Coronation festivities this happened in the case of the sister of the Khedive of Egypt, who showed me and allowed me to handle some of the finest pearls in the world, amongst which were specimens as large as pigeons’ eggs. She showed me, amongst other things, the black pearls presented to her by the late King Edward on his return from India. Again, just before the Russo-Japanese war Prince David Beboutoff, when negotiating a loan in this country, deposited here share certificates worth close on a million of money. This was only one deposit out of thousands which take place every year. We have had the title deeds, securities, and other property lodged here of fifty people who have died and whose property has been valued for probate at upwards of £5,000,000.’”

“An inspection of Messrs. Harrods’ Safe Deposit Department is a revelation of fire and burglar resisting devices. The most cunning thief might as well try to wrest valuable mineral from the moon as steal gold from these vaults, which are a maze of time-locks, steel doors, steel and wrought iron bars, joists, and floors, whilst, outside, the arrangements for swamping the outer skin of the premises with water are perfect. These stores are distinguished as being the first in this or any other country to add to their other conveniences a Safe Deposit Department.”
